subject: ARP address resolution

source.locator: Packet Generation / Packet Reception / An Example

authored.protocol: source-first: the author agent read only RFC 826 and never saw the .fd file

questions.ask: When the requesting host cannot resolve a target host's hardware address, how is the resulting ARP request packet addressed when it goes out on the Ethernet — to one specific station, or to every station on the segment?
questions.tests: the initial ARP request is broadcast, not sent to a single host
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Generation: "It then causes this packet to be broadcast to all stations on the Ethernet cable originally determined by the routing mechanism."
questions.answer: The request is broadcast to all stations on the Ethernet cable/segment; it is not addressed to any single specific host.

questions.ask: What is missing from the requesting host's own state, before it sends anything, that causes it to broadcast an ARP request in the first place?
questions.tests: a cache miss at the requester (no existing mapping for the target) triggers the request
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Generation and An Example: "...because X was just started, it does not have this information. It throws the Internet packet away and instead creates an ADDRESS RESOLUTION packet..."
questions.answer: The requester's own translation table does not yet hold a mapping from the target's protocol address to the target's hardware address, so it discards the packet it was trying to send and generates an ARP request instead.

questions.ask: When the target host receives the ARP request, what two pieces of information from that packet does it store together as an entry in its own table?
questions.tests: the target caches the requester's <protocol address, hardware address> pair taken from the sender fields of the request
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Reception: "...add the triplet <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> to the translation table."
questions.answer: It stores the requester's protocol address (e.g. its IP address) together with the requester's hardware (Ethernet) address, taken from the sender fields of the request packet.

questions.ask: If a host on the segment receives the broadcast request but is not the target protocol address, does it send any reply packet back?
questions.tests: only the target replies; other hosts on the segment that see the broadcast stay silent
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Reception: negative conditionals end processing and discard the packet when the "Am I the target protocol address?" check fails.
questions.answer: No. Only the host whose protocol address matches the target address sends a reply; any other host that receives the broadcast does not respond, and processing simply ends.

questions.ask: When the target host sends its reply back, is that reply broadcast to the whole segment, or sent directly to just the requesting host?
questions.tests: the reply is unicast back to the requester, unlike the broadcast request
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, An Example: "...sends the packet directly (not broadcast) to EA(X)."
questions.answer: The reply is sent directly to the requesting host's hardware address; it is not broadcast to the rest of the segment.

questions.ask: After the requesting host receives the target's reply, what does it do with that information, and what results in its own table?
questions.tests: resulting cache state at the requester once the exchange completes
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, An Example: "Machine X gets the reply packet from Y, forms the map from <ET(IP), IPA(Y)> to EA(Y), notices the packet is a reply and throws it away."
questions.answer: The requester adds a mapping from the target's protocol address to the target's hardware address in its own translation table, then discards the reply packet since it recognizes it as a REPLY.

questions.ask: In the original request packet, does the requesting host already know the target's hardware address, or is that precisely the information the request is meant to obtain?
questions.tests: the target hardware address is unknown/don't-care in the request, because it is exactly what is being resolved
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Generation: "It does not set ar$tha to anything in particular, because it is this value that it is trying to determine."
questions.answer: The requester does not know the target's hardware address yet; that is exactly the value the request is trying to determine, so the field for it is left unset (or optionally set to the broadcast address) in the request.

questions.ask: When a host receives an address-resolution request, does it merge the sender's address mapping into its own table before or after it looks at whether the opcode is a request or a reply?
questions.tests: order of operations: the sender's mapping is merged before the opcode is examined
questions.source_locator: RFC 826, Packet Reception: "Notice that the <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> triplet is merged into the table before the opcode is looked at."
questions.answer: Before — the receiving host merges/updates the sender's protocol-to-hardware address mapping in its table first, and only afterward examines whether the packet is a request or a reply.

none_of: after it looks at the opcode

questions.ask: How long does the requesting host keep the mapping it has just learned before that entry must be re-resolved?
questions.tests: Refusal to hallucinate a lifetime. The presented text shows a cache table with a before state and an after state and carries no notion of time at all.
questions.source_locator: RFC 826 (the address resolution cache and its ageing are described, but no interval is normative) - in scope for the subject, absent from the presented text
questions.answer: NOT STATED. The text shows the cache before and after the exchange and says nothing about how long an entry lives or when it must be refreshed.

questions.ask: Both hosts here are on one segment. What does the text say happens when the target host is on a different segment, reached through a router?
questions.tests: Refusal to import a true fact from knowledge. Every reader knows address resolution is link-local and stops at a router; the presented text draws one segment and licenses no statement about a second one.
questions.source_locator: RFC 826 operates within one link; the router case (proxy resolution, or resolution of the first-hop router instead) is outside anything the presented text carries
questions.answer: NOT STATED. The text draws a single segment and its hosts, and says nothing at all about a router, a second segment, or how resolution behaves across one.
